# Benchmarks for AI (LLM) creativity

Yes, there are benchmark papers on creativity. Since about 2022, researchers have built benchmarks and test batteries to measure the creativity of large language models (LLMs). Most adapt instruments from human creativity research: the Alternate Uses Task (AUT), the Torrance Tests (TTCT), the Divergent Association Task (DAT) and the Consensual Assessment Technique. Others define new, domain-specific scores for code, mathematics, problem solving and research ideas. A parallel line of empirical work asks a different question: does using LLMs make creative output more **similar** across people and across models? That question is called homogenization.

This note catalogues both lines of work. The broader field, the evaluation frameworks of Ritchie and Jordanous, and the human–AI comparisons by Koivisto & Grassini (2023), Hubert et al. (2024) and Doshi & Hauser (2024) are in [[computational-creativity]]. Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (2024) is covered in [[llm-homogenization]].

| Goes et al. — "Pushing GPT's creativity" | 2023, ICCC | Divergent thinking | Whether multi-step "forceful" prompting raises GPT-4's creativity | AUT + adapted TTCT visual completion | Automated, GPT-based evaluation prompts | Forceful prompts improved creativity | Yes |

| **MacGyver** (Tian et al.) | 2024, NAACL | Physical problem solving | Creative, unconventional use of objects under constraints | Creative problem solving; divergent–convergent prompting tested | Human annotators (MTurk) with 6 categories (feasible, efficient, etc.) | Hard for both groups. | Peeperkorn et al. — temperature | 2024, ICCC | Narrative generation | Effect of sampling temperature on creativity | Novelty, typicality, cohesion, coherence | Automated measures + analysis | Temperature is only weakly linked to novelty and moderately linked to incoherence. | **NeoCoder / NeoGauge** (Lu, Wang et al.) | 2025, NAACL | Code (Codeforces) | Convergent + divergent creativity under escalating constraints ("Denial Prompting") | Convergent/divergent thinking (citing Runco) | Automated: correctness × share of techniques absent from human solutions | Even GPT-4 falls short of human-like creativity. Advanced reasoning strategies did not help significantly | Yes |
| **Creativity Index** (Lu, Sclar et al.) | 2025, ICLR (oral) | Novels, poetry, speeches | Linguistic novelty: how much of a text *cannot* be rebuilt from web text | Novelty as non-reconstructibility (no classic test) | Automated n-gram attribution (DJ Search) against a web corpus | Professional authors score on average 66.2% higher than LLMs. Alignment lowers LLM scores by 30.1% | Yes |

## Per-benchmark notes

- **Stevenson et al. (2022).** This is one of the first LLM–AUT comparisons. GPT-3 responses were compared with earlier human responses on expert ratings and on semantic distance from the object. The authors expected GPT-3 to "catch up" on this task.
- **Goes et al. (2023).** This is a *prompting* study, not a fixed benchmark. GPT-4 critiques and improves its own AUT and TTCT-style answers over several conversational turns.
- **Gómez-Rodríguez & Williams (2023).** The prompt is deliberately unusual: Ignatius J. Reilly from *A Confederacy of Dunces* fights a pterodactyl. The goal was to avoid training-data reuse. Open-source models lagged behind. Humor split the models into those that handle it about as well as humans and those that fail.
- **TTCW (Chakrabarty et al., 2024).** This moves Torrance's process dimensions to the *product* (the story) and scores them with expert consensus, in the way of the CAT. The 48 stories were written either by professional authors or by LLMs. The experiment with LLMs as automatic assessors failed: none correlated positively with the experts.
- **MacGyver (Tian et al., 2024).** The dataset has 1,683 problems, 1,306 solvable and 377 unsolvable. Each answer was annotated by three MTurk workers. Majority-vote correctness was 79.3% for humans and 73.3% for GPT-4. With a single random answer, GPT-4 scored 62.4% and humans 65.1%. Humans do well on familiar tasks but lack specialist knowledge. LLMs attempt more but propose infeasible actions. Iterative step-wise reflection and divergent–convergent prompting helped.
- **Peeperkorn et al. (2024).** This is not a benchmark but a test of a common assumption: that temperature controls creativity. One fixed context, model and prompt were sampled across temperatures.
- **NeoCoder (Lu, Wang et al., 2025).** There are 199 recent Codeforces problems, each with 30 correct human solutions. Denial Prompting forbids the techniques of the previous solution for up to 5 rounds. Convergent creativity = passes all tests *and* respects the constraints. Divergent creativity = share of the solution's techniques never used in the human solutions. Eight models were tested, including GPT-4, Claude 3 Sonnet and Llama 3 70B.
- **Creativity Index (Lu, Sclar et al., 2025).** A word counts as unique if no n-gram of length ≥ L containing it appears in the reference corpus (RedPajama). The index is the area under the uniqueness curve across L. The gap is largest for speeches. RLHF alignment lowers LLM scores. The same score also works as a strong zero-shot detector of machine text.
- **CreativeMath (Ye et al., 2025).** The full set has 6,469 problems and 14,223 solutions from AMC 8 up to the IMO. Experiments used 400 problems. A solution counts as novel only if it is correct and distinct from the k reference solutions shown. It is then classified as "Novel-Unknown" if it also differs from all other known human solutions.
- **Si et al. (2025).** This is a large expert evaluation, not an automatic benchmark. The authors list "lack of diversity in generation" and failures of LLM self-evaluation as open problems.
- **Zhao et al. (2025).** This adapts the modified TTCT to LLMs with an LLM evaluator. Collaboration among several LLMs raised originality.
- **Ismayilzada et al. (2025).** The study compares 60 LLMs with 60 people on a cue-word story task. Expert ratings broadly agreed with the automated metrics, but non-experts and LLMs did not. That gap matters for any benchmark that uses LLM-as-judge.
- **LiveIdeaBench (Ruan et al., 2026).** It explicitly operationalizes Guilford's divergent-thinking criteria. It is called "live" because both the judge panel and the keywords can be refreshed. For example, QwQ-32B-preview performed comparably to claude-3.7-sonnet:thinking despite large gaps in general-intelligence scores.

## Homogenization findings

These studies measure **between-person or between-model similarity** rather than the quality of individual outputs.

| Study | Venue | Design | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Padmakumar & He (2024) | ICLR 2024 | Argumentative essays written with GPT3, with InstructGPT, or without AI | Writing with InstructGPT, but not GPT3, significantly reduced diversity. Essays converged mainly because the model's contributed text was less diverse. Quality gains from feedback-tuning may cost diversity. |
| Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (2024) | C&C '24 | 36-participant ideation study, ChatGPT vs an alternative creativity support tool | Different users produced less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT. See [[llm-homogenization]]. |
| Doshi & Hauser (2024) | *Science Advances* | Story writing with GPT-4 ideas | Individual creativity rose while collective diversity fell. See [[computational-creativity]]. |
| Kumar et al. (2025) | CHI 2025 | Two pre-registered experiments, 1,100 participants, AUT (divergent) and RAT (convergent) | LLM help boosted performance while assisted but may hinder later *unassisted* performance. People exposed to LLM-generated strategies kept producing more similar ideas even without the LLM. |
| Wenger & Kenett (2026) | *PNAS Nexus* | Many humans and many LLMs on standardized tasks (AUT, Forward Flow and DAT in the arXiv version) | LLM responses resemble *other LLMs'* responses far more than humans resemble other humans, even after controls. Switching models would not escape homogenization. |
| Si et al. (2025) | ICLR 2025 | LLM ideation agent | Lack of diversity in generation is an open problem (see above). |

The cross-model result (Wenger & Kenett) and the persistence result (Kumar et al.) extend the single-tool, single-session design of Anderson et al. (2024).

## Patterns and limitations

- **Average vs top performers.** Several large comparisons find LLMs at or above the *average* human but below the best or more creative humans (Bellemare-Pepin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). This matches Koivisto & Grassini (2023) in [[computational-creativity]].
- **Divergent-thinking tests vs expert product judgement.** LLMs do well on AUT/DAT-style tasks, but expert-judged product benchmarks favour professionals (Chakrabarty et al., 2024; Lu, Sclar et al., 2025; Ismayilzada et al., 2025).
- **LLM-as-judge is fragile.** In TTCW no LLM judge correlated positively with experts (Chakrabarty et al., 2024). LLM and non-expert raters overrate LLM stories relative to experts (Ismayilzada et al., 2025). Si et al. (2025) report failures of LLM self-evaluation. CreativeMath and LiveIdeaBench nonetheless rely on LLM judges.
- **Contamination / memorization.** Several designs exist mainly to stop models from retrieving training data: unusual prompts (Gómez-Rodríguez & Williams, 2023), escalating constraints (Lu, Wang et al., 2025; Atmakuru et al., 2024), and explicit web attribution (Lu, Sclar et al., 2025).
- **Alignment may trade diversity for quality.** This is reported for co-writing diversity (Padmakumar & He, 2024) and for the Creativity Index (Lu, Sclar et al., 2025).
- **Simple knobs are weak.** Temperature is only weakly linked to novelty (Peeperkorn et al., 2024). Persona prompting helped only up to a threshold, beyond which output departed from real-life patterns, and strategic prompt engineering gave mixed to negative results (Wang et al., 2025). Prompting and temperature *did* raise semantic divergence for some models (Bellemare-Pepin et al., 2026).
- **Product, not process.** Almost all benchmarks score outputs. The survey by Ismayilzada, Paul et al. (preprint, below) calls for process-driven, multi-dimensional evaluation.

## Preprints (not peer-reviewed)

- **CS4** (Atmakuru et al., 2024) — preprint, not peer-reviewed. It is reportedly linked to an EMNLP 2024 workshop, but we could not find it in the ACL Anthology volume of that workshop. 50 instructions each expanded to up to 39 constraints. Tested LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral and OLMo.
- **Holzner, Maier & Feuerriegel (2025)** meta-analysis — preprint, not peer-reviewed. It pools 28 studies (8,214 participants). GenAI vs humans: no significant difference (g = −0.05). Humans with GenAI vs without: g = 0.27. Effect of GenAI on the diversity of ideas in human–AI collaboration: g = −0.86.
- **Moon, Green & Kushlev (2024–2025)** "Homogenizing effect of LLMs on creative diversity: human vs ChatGPT writing" — preprint (PsyArXiv), not peer-reviewed. We found no journal version, so its findings are not used here.
- **Ismayilzada, Paul, Bosselut & van der Plas (2024)** "Creativity in AI: Progresses and Challenges" — preprint (survey), not peer-reviewed. Its conclusion: models produce linguistically and artistically creative outputs but struggle with creative problem solving, abstraction and compositionality, and their outputs lack diversity and originality.

## Connections

- [[computational-creativity]]: the field, evaluation frameworks (Ritchie; Jordanous's SPECS) and the first LLM-vs-human studies. This note adds the dedicated benchmarks.
- [[llm-homogenization]]: the full treatment of Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (2024). The homogenization table above places it among later studies.
- [[measuring-creativity]]: the human instruments (AUT, TTCT, DAT, CAT) that most benchmarks adapt. Note the shift from process tests to product ratings (TTCW).
- [[divergent-convergent-thinking]]: NeoGauge, MacGyver, Kumar et al. and LiveIdeaBench operationalize this pair explicitly.
- [[boden-three-types]]: the Creativity Index and CreativeMath's "Novel-Unknown" category approximate H-novelty relative to a corpus. Most benchmarks test combinational or exploratory creativity, not transformational.
- [[definition]]: almost all benchmarks score novelty plus value (correctness, feasibility, coherence). Ismayilzada et al. add surprise.
